rationale: A wins because it treats the unknowns as unknowns instead of turning them into copy. Its strongest line, 'Faire starts underwriting its own retailers' inventory - and takes the credit risk off the brands,' is backed by a proof list that asks for default rate, cost, capitalization, and clawback terms. B has a better missing protagonist in the brand angle, but it poisons the well with 'no bank required' and 'Faire isn't using a credit bureau,' neither of which is in the update. That is how a decent angle set becomes a trust problem.
gaps_in_A: 'A $12.6B private marketplace is quietly becoming a lender to 700,000 small businesses' overstates the reach. Faire connects 700,000 retailers; the update does not say all qualify for or will use financing.
'credit institution' is a little hot. The facts support Faire underwriting 60-day terms, not a regulatory or balance-sheet identity unless capitalization and risk terms are disclosed.
The trend angle admits its own weakness: 'there is no supplied current news peg about B2B BNPL or platform lending.' Fine as a sidebar, soft as a lead.
A leaves a real fourth angle on the floor: it notes 'brands are paid upfront while retailers pay later' but never builds a supplier/wholesale-terms story around the 100,000+ brands.
gaps_in_B: 'no bank required' is invented. The update does not disclose whether Faire funds this on its balance sheet, through a bank facility, or with a partner.
'Faire isn't using a credit bureau' is unsupported. 'Underwritten using the retailer's order history' does not exclude bureau data or other credit signals.
'purchase frequency and order history' adds a model feature the update never gave. Order history is supplied; purchase frequency is your decoration.
'Faire absorbs all the default risk' is too absolute. Brands are paid upfront, but clawbacks, enforcement, collections, and risk allocation are not disclosed.
